planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with shelter from strong wind; the arching branches and pendulous flower clusters are shown off best when sited where lower limbs can sweep near the ground.

directions: Epaulette Tree is a small deciduous Styracaceae relative of Styrax and Halesia, native to woodland margins in Japan, China, and Korea, grown for its long, drooping, wisteria-like panicles of small fragrant white flowers that hang beneath the branches in late spring. The common name comes from the clusters of bristly, hairy seed capsules that follow the flowers and resemble military shoulder epaulettes, adding an unusual textural feature into autumn. It performs best as an understory specimen in filtered light with consistently moist, well-drained soil, and benefits from underplanting that hides its sometimes leggy lower trunk. Established trees are relatively low-maintenance and are mostly found through specialty and arboretum-affiliated nurseries rather than mainstream retail.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this smaller relative of the Epaulette Tree fits woodland borders and shrub groupings where the larger Pterostyrax hispida would outgrow the space.

directions: Littleleaf Epaulette Tree is a large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree native to Japanese woodlands, closely related to the better-known Pterostyrax hispida but staying considerably smaller and bearing its fragrant white flowers in rounded, upright corymbs rather than long drooping racemes. Clusters of small, bristly fruit follow the late-spring bloom and persist into fall, giving the plant a secondary season of interest against its clean oval foliage. It prefers the same moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland conditions as its relatives and is rarely seen outside arboreta and specialty plant collections. Underplant with shade perennials to disguise the open base typical of young plants as it matures into a graceful multi-stemmed form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, giving the same protected woodland-edge siting used for the related North American silverbells.

directions: MacGregor's Silverbell is a Chinese counterpart to the familiar Carolina Silverbell, native to mixed woodlands of central and western China, and hangs similar white, bell-shaped flowers from its branches in spring before the leaves fully expand. It is distinguished from the American species mainly by its winged fruit, which carries two wings rather than the four found on Halesia tetraptera, and by slightly narrower, more pointed leaves. Cultivation needs mirror those of the American silverbells: moist, humus-rich, acidic soil, partial shade, and protection from late freezes that can damage emerging flower buds. It remains uncommon in North American gardens and is found mainly through botanical garden plant sales and collector-focused nurseries.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; the small scale and twiggy habit suit woodland borders, rock gardens, and mixed shrub beds better than the larger tree-form Styrax species.

directions: Wilson's Snowbell is a compact, densely twiggy deciduous shrub native to woodland slopes in western China, staying far smaller than tree-form relatives like Japanese Snowbell. Small, nodding, bell-shaped white flowers open along the branches in late spring, set against small rounded leaves that give the whole plant a fine, airy texture. It shares the genus's preference for moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil and dappled shade, and works well layered beneath larger understory trees such as Halesia or Stewartia. It is seldom offered commercially and is mostly obtained through specialty shrub nurseries or botanical garden sales.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; the weeping branch structure is most effective sited where it can be viewed from below or beside a path, patio, or pond.

directions: Snow Cascade is a weeping selection of the popular Japanese Snowbell, bred to cascade its branches downward rather than growing in the species' typical broad, horizontally tiered form. Fragrant, bell-shaped white flowers dangle in rows along the pendulous branches in late spring, creating a curtain effect that is especially striking planted above a slope, wall, or walkway where the blooms can be viewed from beneath. Like the species, it prefers moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and benefits from partial shade in hotter climates to prevent leaf scorch. Light structural pruning when young helps establish a strong leader before the weeping habit fully takes over.
sources: J.C. Raulston Arboretum at NC State University
